assessments.reasoning: Page 60 gives two sufficient header forms for locality, an explicit LOCAL following the name or a parameter list. It confines ordinary declared variables to that procedure even when names recur elsewhere. Page 61 gives the global-name spelling for declarations and references, placing the underscore after $, # or &. These passages support the stated binding rule. Separate evidence would be needed to document the return-argument colon itself from this case.

challenge.method: Check the default header, an argument-bearing header without LOCAL, and an explicitly global name inside a local procedure.
challenge.results: The default is global. Declaring arguments suffices for locality, and the global-name rule limits the ordinary procedure-scope statement. The spelling rule supplies no general permission to declare every kind of variable in every context.

limitations: The global spelling applies to the three named variable markers, subject to the declaration and reference rules for each marker.
The chapter assigns a separate purpose to the colon prefix on procedure arguments returned to a caller. Variable retention and query column-binding rules are separate.

Independently reviewed as a descriptive report of Oracle's October 2022 PeopleTools 8.60 documentation. No PeopleTools SQR runtime execution, other version coverage or independent source corroboration was used.

The cited global spelling is subject to the underlying command and variable-family rules. In particular, the reference catalogs errors 007209 and 007211 for prohibited typed declaration forms. The revision does not promise that adding an underscore permits a global DECLARE-VARIABLE statement inside a procedure.

Chapter 1 distinguishes & database-column/expression names, $ text/date names, # numeric names, % list names and @ marker-location names. This result is limited to the three markers named in the cited global spelling rule. Argument return, query-column binding and variable retention are separate behaviors.
